transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well... I guess the main reason is that I’ve gotten myself into a bit of a corner. I’m an artist, and lately I’ve been saying yes to everything—projects, workshops, studio improvements, client calls, all of it. At first it felt productive, like I was finally getting momentum and catching up on all the things I’d been meaning to do, but now it’s gotten to the point where I can’t realistically manage it all.

I’ve got deadlines stacked on top of deadlines, people expecting things from me, and I keep looking around the studio thinking, “Why did I start all of this at once?” And then there’s the mortgage, which is becoming this constant pressure in the background. So I came in because it’s starting to feel like everything is closing in on me, and I’m worried I’ve taken on far more than I can actually handle.
During this period of saying yes to everything, have you been needing much less sleep than usual?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, my sleep has been… disrupted in the sense that I’ll stay up later because I’m trying to finish things, or I’ll lie there thinking through what I’ve promised people, what needs to be framed, what emails I haven’t answered, that sort of thing.

But needing less sleep, like genuinely feeling fine on very little sleep—I don’t know. I haven’t really been tracking it carefully. Some nights I probably do sleep less, but I can’t tell if that’s because I don’t need it or because I’m just pushing myself and worrying. I wouldn’t want to say yes confidently, because I’m not sure.
During this time, have you been feeling unusually high, euphoric, or more upbeat than is typical for you?

Yes… I think I have, actually. Not “happy” in a normal, calm way exactly, but more like I felt lit up. Most days it was like everything suddenly had possibility again—the studio, the garden, the work I’d been putting off. I’d look around and think, “Yes, this is finally coming together, I can make all of this work,” and there was this buoyant feeling, like I was moving with the current instead of against it.

But it wasn’t all pleasant. If someone interrupted that or questioned whether I could really manage it, or asked about invoices or practical details, I could get sharp very quickly. Sharper than I’d like to admit. It felt like they were puncturing the whole thing, like they didn’t understand the momentum I had. So yes, more upbeat and energized than usual, but also much more easily irritated if anyone challenged the plan.
During this period, have you been more driven than usual to start or take on lots of projects?

Yes. Very much so. That’s honestly one of the main reasons I’m here, because I didn’t just take on one or two extra things—I started agreeing to everything that came near me.

It was projects, commissions, workshops, things for the studio I’d been meaning to fix or reorganize, calls with clients, follow-ups, planning sessions… and at the time each one felt important and doable. I remember thinking, “If I just keep going, I can get all of this moving.” But now when I actually look at the calendar, it’s ridiculous. The deadlines are all stacked together, and people are waiting on me, and I’ve created this huge amount of pressure for myself.

And the mortgage is there in the background too, so part of me kept thinking I should say yes because I need the work, I need the income, I need to keep things afloat. But I’ve taken on far more than I can realistically manage. It’s like I kept starting and committing before stopping to ask whether there was any actual room in my life to finish it all.
During this period, have you felt more confident in your abilities than is usual for you?

Yes… yes, I think so. More than I realized at the time.

It wasn’t just ordinary confidence, like, “I’m good at what I do” or “I can handle this commission.” It got much bigger than that in my head. I started thinking my illustration work wasn’t just useful or distinctive, but that it could become this whole visual language that scientific journals had somehow been missing for decades. Like there was this gap no one had properly understood, and suddenly I could see it clearly.

And the strange part is, I didn’t just think, “Maybe I have something to contribute.” I felt oddly certain that I was the person who could pull it off. Not just one of many artists who might help, but almost like I had a particular ability to translate things visually in a way other people hadn’t managed. At the time it felt inspiring and completely reasonable, but saying it out loud now, I can hear how inflated it sounds.
During this period, were you talking noticeably more than usual?

Yes, I think I was. I didn’t notice it at first because in my mind I was just explaining things clearly, you know, getting all the pieces out before they disappeared. But in meetings especially, I could hear myself going faster and faster.

I’d start with one simple thing, like a layout for an illustration, and then suddenly I’d be talking about pigments, and symbols, and how the margins should work, and what the budget might need to be, and how it all connected to the bigger purpose of the project. It was like everything was linked and I had to say all of it right then.

And people did interrupt me. Not rudely, usually, but they had to sort of cut in because I wasn’t leaving any space for them to answer. I’d ask a question and then keep talking before they could respond. At the time I thought they just weren’t following quickly enough, but looking back, I can see I was probably overwhelming them.
During this period, have you felt unusually driven to keep working or creating, beyond your normal level?

Yes, definitely. It felt like there was this… humming current in me from the moment I woke up, like I couldn’t just have coffee and sit quietly or ease into the day. I’d go straight into the studio and start moving things around, rearranging shelves, pulling out supplies, making lists, then rewriting the lists because suddenly the first version didn’t seem organized enough.

And it wasn’t only the actual art. I was drafting proposals, emailing people, following up on things that probably could have waited, fiddling with materials, checking pigments and paper and tools, then deciding the whole workspace needed to be changed so I could work “properly.” It all felt urgent, like if I stopped, I’d lose the thread.

Sitting still felt almost impossible. Even when I wasn’t producing anything finished, I was still doing something around the work—sorting, planning, adjusting, preparing. At the time I told myself it was productivity, but it had this restless quality to it that didn’t feel like my usual way of creating.
During this period, did things get so severe that you had to be hospitalized?

I… I don’t think so. Not that I remember, anyway. I mean, it felt intense and unsettling in hindsight, and I know other people were concerned about how I was behaving, but I wasn’t taken to a hospital or admitted anywhere.

There were moments where things probably looked worse from the outside than I understood at the time, but as far as hospitalization, no. I stayed at home and kept trying to manage things there, even if I wasn’t doing it very well.
During that period, did you have any beliefs that other people said were not true or unrealistic?

Yes… I mean, at the time I wouldn’t have called them unrealistic. I felt completely certain. Looking back, I can see how extreme it must have sounded.

I became convinced that a couple of clients — and even one editor I’d worked with — were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled this whole system I thought I was building. It wasn’t just a vague worry, either. I would read into little things, like the way someone worded an email, or if they asked to see progress images, or if they seemed too interested in how the pieces connected. In my mind it all pointed to them trying to get in early, before I was ready, almost like they wanted to take it or interfere with it.

They did reassure me. More than once, actually. They’d say, “No, we just need to understand the direction,” or “We’re not asking for anything beyond the usual,” and part of me heard the words, but it didn’t settle me. I kept thinking, well, of course they’d say that if they were trying to get close to it.

So yes, other people definitely told me I was overreacting or that it wasn’t what was happening. But at the time it felt very real to me.
